comments.text:
🎯 Key Takeaways for quick navigation:

00:00 🧬 对数字实体构建的思考
- 思考如何构建具有人类全部认知工具的数字实体。
- 认为需要某种“潜在抵抗力”来规划和反思。
01:08 🧠 人脑与AI结构的对比
- AI或AGI的构建与人脑结构的相似性。
- 提出了关于记忆、意识以及它们在操作系统中的类比。
02:05 💡 MemGPT作为操作系统的概念介绍
- MemGPT将LLMs视为新型操作系统的核心过程。
- 与传统操作系统的内存管理机制类比，提出虚拟上下文管理的概念。
03:18 💾 记忆系统与操作系统的存储类比
- 讨论了LLMs当前的记忆限制，如上下文窗口的限制。
- 提出MemGPT通过不同记忆层级的智能管理，有效扩展上下文窗口。
07:41 🧠 MemGPT与GPT的记忆功能差异
- MemGPT能够持久记忆信息，而GPT则会快速遗忘。
08:07 💾 MemGPT的内存模型介绍
- 解释了MemGPT的主要上下文（类似RAM）和外部上下文（类似磁盘存储）。
- 描述了GPT-4的不同模型及其最大token容量。
09:03 📖 令牌化(Tokenization)的基础
- 英语中的大多数单词会被视为一个token。
- 更长的单词可能会被分解成多个tokens。
09:31 🗃️ 上下文窗口和系统消息的影响
- 讨论了最大上下文窗口的概念，包括输入、输出以及通常不可见的系统消息或预设提示。
- 指出预设提示可能占用大量tokens。
10:25 🔗 递归总结的问题和影响
- 递归总结虽简单，但会逐渐丢失信息。
- 以YouTube视频质量递减作为递归总结丢失细节的比喻。
11:49 🧩 MemGPT的工作上下文管理示例
- 展示了MemGPT如何从对话中提取关键信息并将其保存。
- 强调了MemGPT在保持对话上下文连贯性方面的优势。
15:44 🧠 MemGPT增强用户参与度
- MemGPT通过存储信息来提高用户参与度和开放性对话的质量。
16:41 📚 MemGPT在文档分析中的应用
- MemGPT可以处理长文档和复杂数据，比传统模型有效。
- 与GPT-3.5和GP4相比，MemGPT在处理大量文档时准确度不降低。
17:51 🤖 LLM作为代理的新用途
- 通过增强记忆流和规划能力，LLM能在互动环境中充当代理。
- 实验显示LLM能够使用网络搜索来回答问题，并控制其网络浏览环境的上下文大小。

comments.author: @DefenderX
comments.text:
I think the recent discovery of a new memory brain cell, that is theorized to be a hybrid between an astrocyte and neuron, will be helpful to find out how we solve the issue that AI's has trouble searching for the right information.
Having a huge library of information does not help if the AI doesn't know how to search for information based on limited context.
The hybrid memory brain cells has functions from both astrocytes and neurons and can determine the pattern of signal transmittance between neurons in the brain.
So what we need to do in the case of AI, is that we need a function that tells the AI how its search will branch out.
This can be done by categorizing information in the training data with tags that can either become turned on or off depending on what is written in the prompt.
Also specific combinations of tags needs to turn on special tags in the training data.
Let's call these specific search tags for patterns.
An AI will need to sort several search patterns based on probability with the highest probability for the best fit will be ranked highest and searched for first, then the second highest probability search pattern etc.
Also, I think the AI should scan the prompt and determine its search pattern as information gets typed in.

All genius ideas are inspired by something nature already does, and does much better.

comments.author: @pmiddlet72
comments.text:
This shouldn't  be terribly surprising - but a step in the right direction in understanding how each cog fits within a working AI. Maybe we'll find a new physics in all of this :)

TL;DR
From the beginning, a context window simply equates to 'short term memory capacity'. If I were to give you a document to read and summarize it for me, could you do it without taking (and by extension 'storing'') some notes? With the exception of those gifted with a superhuman photographic memory, yeah, in the cog sci sphere the thought is that short-term mem (the RAM analogue) for multitasking, short-term  breakdown of complex tasks, etc - a) it is a mind strategy to chunk information - but what happens when we reach capacity in the number of chunks we can keep in short-term memory (STM)? The things that our brains attend sufficiently enough will go to longer term memory (LTM) (i.e. storage). Ok then b) we must store (the 'taking notes on pencil/paper' analogue) these edited or chunked components thoughtfully. 

Of course now we have to go into the retrieval process in LTM - and this is where things can get a bit complicated (as if the above weren't enough). For information that has been stored in LTM in our brains  hasn't been attended (retrieved) for some time - the specifics of those memory may degrade over time. The machine equivalent is likely to be more persistent in this regard, but it still must make the association with the 'right' stored memory to retrieve for further processing. That's where say, a database, or hard disk comes in (i.e. there may not be an RDBMS, but document based storage is certainly a modern DB paradigm - think S3 et al. ). 

Now what becomes problematic for the machine is finding the 'right' LTM object that fits the current context in which the machine is being interacted. For a human, that can be time consuming (with a bunch of 'ummms' and 'uhhhhs'). For the AI, it would also be more resource intensive, but likely more efficient  - at this time anyway. Traditionally, 'indexing' has been a way for retrieval from databases (a form of LTM) to be more efficient. No doubt an AI would need to use a similar tactic to be efficient AND accurate at LTM retrieval - namely because the human nature of HCI is 'give it to me quickly - I have a 3 second attention span'. 


I think MemGPT handles this in some regard. It's a step in the right direction at least.  As HCI sessions pile on however, that LTM starts becoming rather large, and moreover, varied - and probably, even with some basic 'indexing' tactic, we would probably see reduced efficiencies and/or possible errors. That's the nature of 'cramming' - works well for the short term, but less so for the long. 

This is where I believe multi-agent frameworks are important. Each agent has a simpler, or more limited persona. In that sense we can recruit a quorum of agents - in essence, taking advantage of the idea of parallelism to allow larger contexts. One (of several) things I've yet  to test is,: with a quorum of agents having to retrieve certain elements out of each agent's LTM : is resource usage worse / more costly, or is it improved? i.e. if I create a 'tiger team' of devs/scientists/lay business folks / etc ,to solve a problem that has quite a history - is value increased with a significant reduction in time-to-solution while maintaining solution integrity / accuracy? The trade off in my mind is the initial 'burst' in the number of resources required for a solution, versus the time required to reach the right solution. This is a simulation and optimization type of problem which will probably vary by a number of things (audience, prompts, domain ... )

comments.author: @clray123
comments.text:
Trust me bro, limited context length is not the main issue with the LLMs. Them outputting hopeless garbage at random times is.

Finally, I've tried the exact approach described in the paper before (letting the LLM autonomously decide when to "store" or "retrieve" information from external storage) and it totally craps out on the LLM's inability to make these decisions at appropriate times (speaking of open source LLMs). It would either store/retrieve everything after every prompt (if trained to do so) or not at all. No intelligence was noticeable whatsoever. So I'm very surprised at the purported good results they rave about in the paper. Probaly a lot of "man behind the curtain" prodding the model to do the right memory action at the right time involved in this.
